drug_class: Proteasome inhibitor (a type of targeted cancer medicine)
purpose: Ixazomib is used to treat multiple myeloma, which is a cancer of the plasma cells in your bone marrow. It is used together with two other medicines called lenalidomide and dexamethasone. It helps slow down or stop the growth of cancer cells in your body.
how_it_works: Your cancer cells rely on a kind of 'garbage disposal system' inside them called a proteasome to stay alive and keep growing. Ixazomib works by blocking this garbage disposal system, so harmful proteins build up inside the cancer cells and cause them to die. Healthy cells are much better at handling this disruption than cancer cells, which is why this medicine can target cancer more specifically.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include diarrhea, constipation, nausea, and vomiting. You may also notice swelling in your hands, feet, or legs, tiredness, a skin rash, or back pain. Your blood counts may drop, which can make you more prone to infections, bruising, or bleeding — your doctor will monitor this with regular blood tests.
warnings: This medicine can lower your blood cell counts, so watch for signs of infection like fever, chills, or unusual tiredness. It can also cause nerve damage (neuropathy), so tell your doctor if you feel tingling, numbness, or pain in your hands or feet. Do not take this medicine if you are pregnant, as it can harm an unborn baby — effective birth control is very important. Avoid grapefruit and St. John's Wort as they can interfere with how the medicine works.
typical_dosing: Ixazomib comes as a capsule that you take by mouth once a week on the same day each week. The usual dose is 4 mg taken on days 1, 8, and 15 of a 28-day treatment cycle — meaning you take it three weeks in a row, then have one week off. Always take it at least one hour before or two hours after eating, and swallow the capsule whole without crushing or chewing it.
